questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes Code Quality Automation?
options: Run untrusted pull-request code in the same job that holds production credentials.
A quality workflow can run project linters, formatters, static analysis, and configuration checks; a failing tool exit code should be visible to reviewers.
Give every job write permission to avoid troubleshooting authorization errors.
Print all environment variables and event payloads to make the run easier to debug.
questions.answer_key: A quality workflow can run project linters, formatters, static analysis, and configuration checks; a failing tool exit code should be visible to reviewers.
questions.explanation: This is the central behavior of code quality automation: A quality workflow can run project linters, formatters, static analysis, and configuration checks; a failing tool exit code should be visible to reviewers. Validate configuration and behavior against the current official reference before production use.

questions.explanation: Linters: Make the check deterministic and fail with a meaningful status when requirements are not met. questions.prompt: How should a reviewer verify a change related to code quality automation?
options: Publish the workflow to production before reviewing its triggers and permissions.
Run a controlled test or static check, inspect the relevant job and step result, and compare the evidence with the stated acceptance criteria.
Assume the workflow is correct as soon as the YAML file is committed.
Retry every failure without looking at the exit code or preserving evidence.
questions.answer_key: Run a controlled test or static check, inspect the relevant job and step result, and compare the evidence with the stated acceptance criteria.
questions.explanation: Reliable verification uses observable evidence. For this lesson, consider: A quality workflow can run project linters, formatters, static analysis, and configuration checks; a failing tool exit code should be visible to reviewers. A syntax check alone cannot prove remote execution, permissions, or deployment behavior.
